title: Kick Shots in Pool: A Beginner's Guide to Escaping Snookers
description: Stuck behind another ball? Learn how a kick shot works, whether it is legal, and a simple mirror trick to aim it, with an easy drill to practice.
body:
Your opponent just left you snookered. The cue ball is tucked behind a blocker, and the object ball is on the far side of the table. Time to give up? Not if you know the kick shot, one of the most useful (and most fun) skills in pool.

What is a kick shot?

A kick shot is any shot where the cue ball bounces off at least one cushion before it hits the ball you are aiming at. Players use it when a straight line to the object ball is blocked, or when they want to escape a safety without handing over a free shot.

Is a kick shot legal?

Yes, as long as you do the basics right. Under the World Pool-Billiard Association (WPA) rules, the cue ball must hit a legal object ball first. After that contact, a ball must be pocketed or some ball must touch a cushion. Hit the right ball first and get a ball to a rail, and the kick is a perfectly good shot. Always check the exact wording of the rules your league or room uses, since details vary by game.

The mirror idea: angles in equals angles out

Here is the simple picture. With a medium-speed stroke and no sidespin, a ball bounces off a cushion at roughly the same angle it came in, like a ray of light off a mirror. That gives you an easy way to aim:

  • Imagine a mirror image. Pretend the rail is a mirror and the object ball has a twin on the other side of it, the same distance behind the cushion.
  • Aim at the twin. Pick the spot on the rail where a straight line from the cue ball to the twin crosses the cushion. That is where your cue ball should hit.
  • Shoot and watch. A smooth stroke sends the cue ball to the rail and then toward the real object ball.

It sounds fancy, but it is the same geometry as a bank shot, just aimed at the cue ball instead of an object ball. If you enjoyed our bank shot and diamond system guide, this will feel familiar.

Stay relaxed, too. Kick shots feel tricky because you cannot see the full path, so take a slow practice stroke, stay down after contact and let the shot finish. Good habits matter more than power here.

Use the diamonds

The little markers on the rails, called diamonds, make the mirror idea easier to see. Most players guess the rail spot by eye, check it against the diamonds, and adjust. Over time you learn the paths your table likes. Every table plays a little differently depending on the cloth, the cushions and even the weather, so treat any formula as a starting point, not a promise.

What changes the angle?

Real tables are not perfect mirrors. These things can bend the path of the cue ball:

  • Sidespin. English changes how the ball grips the cushion and leaves it. Our spin guide explains how it works.
  • Speed. A soft shot and a hard shot rarely leave the rail on the same line, so keep your pace steady and the same every time while you learn.
  • Cloth and cushions. New cloth, old cloth, a damp room or a sticky rail can all change the bounce.

The best fix is practice. Set up the same kick shot five times and see where the ball goes. Then change one thing at a time.

A simple practice drill

  1. Place an object ball near the middle of a long side and put the cue ball near the opposite corner.
  2. Pick one rail to kick off and aim using the mirror idea.
  3. Use a smooth, medium stroke with no sidespin. Try ten shots.
  4. Count how many times you hit the object ball first. Try to beat that score next session.
  5. Then try two-rail kicks once one-rail kicks feel easy.

When to kick

A kick is a defensive tool as much as an offensive one. When you are hiding behind a ball, a well-placed kick can hit the object ball and leave your opponent with a hard shot, which fits right in with our safety play guide. Just remember the rule: you have to hit the right ball first, and something has to reach a rail afterward.

Keep learning

Watching the pros makes kick shots click. Check the big tournaments page to see what is coming up, look through the tournament finder for a local event, or browse the guides for more beginner help. When you hear the crowd gasp after a kick, now you will know why.

Quick recap

  • A kick shot bounces the cue ball off a rail before it hits the object ball.
  • Hit the legal ball first, then make sure a ball is pocketed or touches a rail.
  • Use the mirror idea to pick your aim, and check it with the diamonds.
  • Sidespin, speed and the table all change the angle, so practice with a steady stroke.
